trimming_rule.rationale: docs/load/artifacts/s2-dry-run-*.ndjson showed a clean bimodal split before any load test ran: every sample fell either under ~2.5s or in a 30-33s band (matching timedatectl offset ~-30s). 10000ms sits in the empty gap between those two populations, so at low concurrency the split is exact, not a percentile guess.
trimming_rule.validity_breaks_down_at_high_concurrency: At s2_capacity vus=100 and vus=200, removed_rate reaches 71.8% and 83.0% (vs ~4-8% everywhere else, matching s0_artifact_baseline). Real queueing latency has grown to overlap and exceed the 10s threshold there, so the trim no longer separates artifact from real latency; treat trimmed.* at those two stages as NOT meaningful (the trim just clips the top of a genuinely-growing distribution) and read raw.* instead, aware raw also carries the ~5% baseline artifact.
trimming_rule.recompute: Every *-raw.ndjson under docs/load/raw/ is kept; rerun tools/k6/lib/trim-node.js summarizeDurations() with a different threshold to disagree with this rule.

environment_limitation.summary: This machine (WSL2 on Windows) has an unstable VM clock: journalctl -k shows recurring "Time jumped backwards, rotating" and timedatectl timesync-status reports System clock synchronized: no with an offset around -30s even after a full wsl --shutdown. A fixed fraction of HTTP requests (see s0_artifact_baseline: 4.2% at 1 VU with essentially no load) stall for ~30-33s end to end.
environment_limitation.ruled_out: http_req_blocked stayed under 0.5ms on every sample (rules out k6 client-side/connection-level causes). All stalled requests in the dry runs still returned 202 (rules out an application-level failure -- the request succeeds, just very late).
environment_limitation.fix_attempted: sudo systemctl restart systemd-timesyncd and a full wsl --shutdown from the Windows host were both tried; neither resolved the offset/jitter (offset stayed within a few seconds of -30s, jitter single-digit seconds, both before and after).
environment_limitation.decision: Per explicit user instruction, further root-cause investigation of the WSL2 clock itself was stopped in favor of characterising the effect (load-independent, ~4-8% of requests, ~30s stall, no effect on correctness) and trimming it out of the reported latency figures using the stated rule above -- with raw figures always kept alongside so the trim is falsifiable.
environment_limitation.portability: The capacity KNEE (where p99 starts climbing relative to earlier stages, where errors start appearing, the shape of the throughput-vs-concurrency curve) is measurable and portable as a qualitative finding. The absolute latency and TPS numbers are NOT portable off this specific machine/run -- a different WSL2 VM, a bare-metal Linux host, or a different day on this same machine would produce different absolute figures.

caveats: LocalStack DynamoDB emulator is a single-process emulator, not real AWS DynamoDB -- its latency characteristics under concurrent transactional load do not represent production DynamoDB.

Only 2 of the 208 seeded accounts (alice/acc-001, bob/acc-002) are "real" fixtures reused from earlier steps; the other 206 are load-test-only ring/exhaustible accounts created by tools/k6/seed/seed-load-test-fixtures.sh.
fraud-service has no runtime latency/failure-injection knob (unlike mock-bacen-spi's AdminConfigController) -- s4_fraud below did not run; see docs/steps/step-64.md (proposed, unimplemented).

No HTTP connection-pool or thread-pool tuning was found in any service's application.yml -- Tomcat runs its Spring Boot default (max-threads=200), which numerically coincides with where s2_capacity errors start appearing (100-200 VUs); flagged as a plausible but unconfirmed cause (no thread-pool metrics were collected).
This is WSL2 on Windows, not bare-metal Linux -- CPU/IO scheduling, and the clock issue above, are both properties of that virtualization layer, not of the application.
